summary:
Riau is a province of Indonesia and stands under the national framework described below. Indonesia is a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, that provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Riau's own provincial record shows no divergence from this national baseline, and no separate provincial criminalisation regime is documented for it. Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women alongside the national morality provisions. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and apply to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors; in Aceh two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025.

Physical risk is rising across the country. Vigilante mobs are attacking transgender people, and a wave of attacks on trans women between 14 and 16 July 2026 included incidents in Bogor, West Java. Reporting in August 2026 ties the surge to officials' public condemnations and to a presidential decree of October 2025 that lists the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture among non-military security threats alongside terrorism and drugs, placing LGBTQ+ people inside national security policy while the government moves to codify anti-LGBTQ+ attitudes into law.

Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue. On 22 June 2025 officers raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman; Amnesty International said the gathering violated no law and called the operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy. In August 2025 police arrested three men over an alleged LGBTQ Facebook community page, with up to 12 years' imprisonment possible if convicted.

Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges; during a WhatsApp call his mother in Lima was told authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody and his mother alleges police beat him. Indonesian police denied that violence was used.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment; in March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal, and the government has blocked websites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ-related words, including Grindr. A bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Indonesia recognises only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors, with no third-gender or X option. Legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval. No national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.
tangentialFactors:
The national picture is uneven in a way that matters for routing. Only Aceh and South Sumatra impose explicit provincial criminalisation of same-sex conduct; elsewhere the exposure runs through the national penal code's extra-marital sex provision, the 2006 pornography law, and public order charges, which is why reporting describes prosecutions as selective rather than systematic.

The escalation documented in 2025 and 2026 is driven from the top rather than from below. A presidential decree of October 2025 classed the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture as a non-military security threat alongside terrorism and drugs, and reporting in August 2026 links that classification directly to the wave of vigilante attacks on trans women of 14–16 July 2026, which reached as far as Bogor in West Java. The same reporting describes a governmental move to write anti-LGBTQ+ attitudes into law, and a bill to prohibit online content presenting LGBT behaviour was still under discussion in 2025.

Enforcement against gatherings has been large-scale and recent: the Puncak villa raid of 22 June 2025 produced 75 arrests from a private event that Amnesty International said broke no law, and the August 2025 arrests over an alleged LGBTQ Facebook page carry a possible 12-year sentence. Online spaces that visitors might use to meet people therefore carry documented legal exposure of their own.

Custody risk is not theoretical. The death in August 2022 of Rodrigo Ventocilla, a foreign visitor arrested at an Indonesian airport, and his mother's allegation of police beating alongside a reported demand for up to US$100,000 for release, stand against the police denial that violence occurred. No comparable case is documented for Riau itself.
localsOnly:
Residents of Riau live under the same national regime as visitors, with the additional burdens of residence. Legal gender recognition on official documents requires sex reassignment surgery and the approval of a judge, and identity documents recognise only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors with no third-gender or X option.

No national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and national law provides no hate-crime protection on those grounds. Provincial records for Riau document no local anti-discrimination instrument filling that gap.

Residents face the extra-marital sex provision of the penal code in force since 2 January 2026, the 2006 pornography law's seven-year maximum for material showing or suggesting same-sex relations, and the broadcasting and website restrictions in force since 2016. The August 2025 prosecution of three men over an alleged LGBTQ Facebook community page, with up to 12 years' imprisonment available, shows that online community administration is itself a chargeable risk.
outOfScopeNotes:
No trans-specific safety finding is documented for Riau in the sources reviewed. The province's entry records no divergence from the national baseline, which means the absence of a local record should be read as unsourced rather than as evidence of lower risk.

One overview states that Indonesia does not criminalise private, consensual same-sex activity, with only Aceh applying sharia-based penalties, while the same source records the penal code provision on sex outside marriage effective 2 January 2026. How those two statements are reconciled in current prosecutorial practice is unresolved in the material available here.

The legal basis for the up-to-12-years exposure in the August 2025 arrests over an alleged LGBTQ Facebook page is not stated in the source and remains unverified.

Nothing in the inventory addresses Riau-specific police practice, access to gender-affirming care, HIV or health services, venues and facilities, or documented violence against trans people within the province. Those gaps are not sourced either way.
